choices.text: indicating that a particular plan would have an effect contrary to the anticipated effect
claiming that a particular plan should not be adopted because, while effective, it would have at least one undesirable consequence
arguing that an alternative plan could achieve a desired result more easily than the plan originally proposed
questioning the assumption that authorities are available who have special knowledge of the problem under discussion
offering a counterexample in order to show that a particular general claim is too broadly stated

notes.body:
The anticipated effect of Inez's plan was people to be *more* willing to buy antiques.

Was Anika saying that Inez's plan would lead to people being *less* willing to buy antiques?

Sure. She doesn't explicitly say that, but Anika is saying that Inez's plan would force them to raise prices on their antiques.

Is it common sense to think, "if you raise the price on your antiques, people will be *less* willing to buy it?"

Yes.

(There might be a voice in your head saying, "Not necessarily! Sometimes people are *more* attracted to buying something because the price is higher, like a Fendi bag, or like really expensive wine." Sure, but that's not the typical association. Businesses offer sales and discounts and coupons in order to create demand, in order to make people *more* willing to buy. They don't raise prices to do that, generally.)

This answer is wicked tempting because "undesirable consequence" is a great match for the Faulty Implications answer we were anticipating.

Anika *did* claim that the plan has at least one undesirable consequence (raising prices).

But she never said the plan would be effective. Effectiveness is measured by whether the Plan achieves its Goal of "making people more willing to buy antiques at the fair".

Since Anika says "I disagree with your prediction", she is saying "I don't think the plan would be effective in making people more willing to buy antiques at the fair".

So that part of the answer is contradicted by Anika's statements.
Anika doesn't offer any alternative plan. She just points out problems with Inez's plan.

Nothing Anika says ever touches on whether there would be appraisers available to judge the authenticity of these antiques.

She just says the appraisers are *unnecessary* (since the customers are already experts), not unavailable.

The only general claim Inez makes is that "in poor economic times, people want to be sure they're getting good value for their money".

A counterexample to that would involve a specific case of poor economic times where someone *didn't* care about getting good value for their money.

Anika doesn't present anything resembling that.

choices.text: asserting that the objection is based on a belief about the reliability of clairvoyance rather than on the nature of knowledge or its definition
asserting that the case of clairvoyance is one of knowledge even though we do not really believe in clairvoyance as a reliable process
arguing against the assumption that clairvoyance is unreliable
explaining that the definition of knowledge is a matter of personal choice
demonstrating that the case of clairvoyance is not a case of knowledge and does not fit the definition of knowledge

notes.body:
Did the author say, the reason for the objection is our belief about the reliability of clairvoyance, not about this definition of knowledge?

Sure, the author said, I agree we would reject (object) to these claims, but we would do so **because** we really do not believe in clairvoyance as a reliable process.

The author asserted that we object because of our beliefs about the reliability of clairvoyance. The final sentence is elaborating that this definition is not the problem, because were we to think that clairvoyance were a reliable process, it would satisfy the definition and we would happily accept calling it knowledge.

The author "agrees that we would reject a clairvoyant person's claim to know certain things based on this power".

In other words, "You're right --- if a clairvoyant person claims to know XYZ via clairvoyance, we'd say you don't know XYZ."

Our author thinks that clairvoyance is **not** a case of knowledge. He only thinks it would switch to being a case of knowledge if we were to switch into considering it a reliable process.

The author accepts (in a plural first person pronoun) that " **we** really do not believe in clairvoyance as a reliable process".

He's not arguing against that assumption. He accepts the assumption that clairvoyance is unreliable.

The author never says the definition is a matter of personal choice. The author is defending this definition against an objection, saying that a supposed counterexample isn't really a counterexample.

But he never explains that "how one defines knowledge is really up to them".

So, so close. The author demonstrates that,

the case of clairvoyance is not a case of **reliable process** and thus does not fit the definition of knowledge.

The author does acknowledge that clairvoyance is not a case of knowledge, but that isn't part of defending the definition. The defense of the definition comes when the author says, "the reason clairvoyance isn't knowledge is because of **reliable process**, not because of **bad definition**."

choices.text: Fewer diseases attack leatherbacks than attack other large aquatic reptiles.
The average life expectancy of sea turtles in general is longer than that of almost all other marine animals.
Most leatherbacks that perish in the wild are killed by predators.
Few zoologists have sufficient knowledge to establish an artificial environment that is conducive to the well-being of captive leatherbacks.
The size of a leatherback is an untrustworthy indicator of its age.

notes.body: A compares leatherbacks with other large aquatic reptiles. The surprise is a comparison between captive leatherbacks and wild ones. Fewer diseases attacking leatherbacks would be true in both places, so it creates no difference between captivity and the wild that could offset the captivity diseases.

B compares sea turtles with other marine animals, which is the wrong comparison. Even if sea turtles live long in general, that is true of captive and wild leatherbacks alike, so it doesn't explain why the extra diseases in captivity fail to lower the captive odds.

This is the something-bad-about-the-wild answer we predicted. Captive leatherbacks face diseases the wild ones never meet. Wild leatherbacks face predators, and C tells us predators kill most of the wild ones that perish. Captive turtles are presumably safe from predators. So each setting has its own main danger, and the odds of reaching full life expectancy can come out about the same.

The move to repeat: when two groups end up equal even though one has an obvious disadvantage, look for a disadvantage on the other side that balances it.

D deepens the paradox. If few zoologists know how to build an environment that is good for captive leatherbacks, captivity sounds even worse for them. That is one more reason to expect captive turtles to die younger, which is the opposite of what we need.

E might tempt you if you suspect the life-expectancy figures are measured badly. But nothing in E says the error affects captive and wild turtles differently. If size is a poor guide to age everywhere, it gives no difference between the two settings, so the surprise remains.

Fewer diseases attack leatherbacks than attack other large aquatic reptiles.
The average life expectancy of sea turtles in general is longer than that of almost all other marine animals.
Most leatherbacks that perish in the wild are killed by predators.
Few zoologists have sufficient knowledge to establish an artificial environment that is conducive to the well-being of captive leatherbacks.
The size of a leatherback is an untrustworthy indicator of its age.

notes.body: This compares leatherbacks to other reptiles. The paradox is internal to leatherbacks — captive vs. wild. Whatever leatherbacks face relative to other species doesn't change why captive and wild leatherbacks happen to have similar survival rates despite their different threat environments.

This says sea turtles outlive most other marine animals. Cool fact, but the paradox is about why leatherbacks have similar life-expectancy odds in captivity and in the wild — within the species. Comparisons to other animals don't address that within-species puzzle.

This balances the scales. Captivity has its own threat — fatal diseases that don't exist in the wild. If captives faced that and wild ones faced nothing, captives would die younger on average. But this answer tells us wild leatherbacks face their own deadly threat: predators. Captive leatherbacks don't deal with predators at all.

So both environments have a major mortality factor — disease in captivity, predators in the wild — and they cancel out, producing similar survival odds in both. That's exactly the kind of answer that resolves a "should be different but isn't" paradox.

This makes the paradox worse, not better. If zoologists struggle to give captive leatherbacks a good environment, captives would be expected to do *even worse* than wild ones — yet they don't. The puzzle becomes more puzzling, not less. We need something that explains why the survival rates come out even, not something that should make them more uneven.

This is about whether you can tell a leatherback's age from its size. That's a research methodology issue. The paradox is about actual survival outcomes — how often each group reaches its maximum life expectancy. The age-indicator question doesn't affect those underlying outcomes.

choices.text: It makes an appeal to a general principle.
It denies the good faith of an opponent.
It relies on evaluating the predictable consequences of a proposal.
It substitutes description for giving a rationale for a policy.
It employs a term on two different occasions in different senses.

notes.body:
Rossi's first sentence is a general rule: it is undemocratic for anyone to live under a government that doesn't represent their interests. Rossi then applies it to one group. Children's interests sometimes differ from their parents', so, by the rule, children need their own representation, which means the vote.

"Appeal to a general principle" is how the LSAT describes this move. When an argument opens with a broad "it is wrong / undemocratic / unfair to ..." claim and then applies it to a specific case, look for this answer.

Rossi speaks first, so there is no opponent yet, and Rossi never questions anyone's honesty or motives. Smith doesn't either: Smith grants Rossi's point about interests and disagrees on the merits. An answer about bad faith needs an accusation in the text, and there is none.

Rossi's argument is about what is democratic, not about what would happen if children voted. Rossi never predicts a single result. Smith's worry that children's conceptions are too simple comes closer to practical concerns, which is why C can feel familiar: it fits the other speaker better.

D can tempt because Rossi's argument is short and sounds like a pair of statements. But Rossi does give a rationale. The policy is "children should have the right to vote." The rationale is the principle (living with unrepresented interests is undemocratic) plus the fact (children's interests sometimes differ from their parents'). Test it: ask Rossi "why should children vote?" Rossi has an answer. An argument that substituted description for a rationale would only describe children or voting and never say why the policy follows.

This describes equivocation: one word used in two senses. The only term Rossi repeats is "interests," and it means the same thing both times: what is good for a person or group. With no shift in meaning, there is no equivocation.

choices.text: It makes an appeal to a general principle.
It denies the good faith of an opponent.
It relies on evaluating the predictable consequences of a proposal.
It substitutes description for giving a rationale for a policy.
It employs a term on two different occasions in different senses.
It makes an appeal to a general principle.
It denies the good faith of an opponent.
It relies on evaluating the predictable consequences of a proposal.
It substitutes description for giving a rationale for a policy.
It employs a term on two different occasions in different senses.

notes.body: This is a clean description of Rossi's move. The argument starts with a broad democratic principle (governments need to represent the interests of those they govern) and then shows it applies to a specific group (children with distinct interests). That's textbook appeal to a general principle.
Rossi doesn't attack anyone's honesty or sincerity. Rossi just makes a positive case from a general principle. There's no opponent being accused of bad faith.

This describes a consequentialist argument — weighing predicted outcomes. Rossi doesn't do that. Rossi argues from principle (representation is owed to those governed) to conclusion (children should vote). The consequence-based reasoning belongs to Smith, not Rossi.

This accuses Rossi of just describing the situation without giving a reason. But Rossi gives a clear reason — the democratic principle of representation. There's a real argument here, not just description.

Rossi doesn't use a word with two different meanings. The argument moves cleanly from principle to application without any term getting redefined along the way. So this isn't a sleight-of-hand argument.

choices.text: The number of amateur musicians who play popular music has decreased.
Most professional musicians are able to play both electric and nonelectric instruments.
The number of professional musicians in some bands has increased.
The total number of professional bands has increased as a result of electrification.
Many professional musicians play in more than one band.

notes.body: The paragraph only counts musicians who play popular music professionally. Amateurs never come up, so we have no information about whether their numbers rose, fell, or stayed the same.

The paragraph says instruments were electrified. It never says whether any musician can play a nonelectric instrument, let alone most of them. A claim about musicians' skills has nothing to stand on here.

This is the most popular wrong answer. The *average* band got smaller. Some bands could have grown, but nothing in the passage says so, and the average would also fall if every single band shrank. An answer that is merely possible isn't supported.

Fewer musicians per band, more musicians overall. The only way both are true is more bands. Picture 100 musicians in bands of 5: 20 bands. Now 150 musicians in bands of 3: 50 bands. Electrification drives both trends, so crediting it with the extra bands is fair.

This is one way to spread musicians across more bands, but nothing in the paragraph says anyone plays in more than one band. The math only forces more bands; it does not tell us how musicians are spread across them. Every musician could play in exactly one band and the facts still hold.

choices.text: The number of amateur musicians who play popular music has decreased.
Most professional musicians are able to play both electric and nonelectric instruments.
The number of professional musicians in some bands has increased.
The total number of professional bands has increased as a result of electrification.
Many professional musicians play in more than one band.
The number of amateur musicians who play popular music has decreased.
Most professional musicians are able to play both electric and nonelectric instruments.
The number of professional musicians in some bands has increased.
The total number of professional bands has increased as a result of electrification.
Many professional musicians play in more than one band.

notes.body: The passage talks about professional musicians and bands. It says nothing about amateurs. So we can't infer anything about amateur numbers — the data isn't there.

The passage doesn't tell us anything about individual musicians' versatility — what kinds of instruments they can play. So we can't support a claim about most musicians being able to play both electric and nonelectric instruments.

This says some bands have grown. The stimulus tells us the average size shrank — it doesn't spotlight bands that grew. While "average shrank" is technically compatible with some bands growing, the passage doesn't affirmatively support that claim. The conclusion isn't there.

This is the math. The stimulus tells us total musicians went up and per-band musicians went down. Run that through: a bigger pool divided into smaller groups gives you more groups. So the number of professional bands must have gone up. And since electrification is what's driving both of those underlying trends in the stimulus, attributing the increase in bands to electrification is fair.
This is about musicians playing in more than one band. The stimulus doesn't bring this up at all. The given facts don't support the claim either way.

choices.text: The National Tea Association has announced that it plans to carry out its own retail survey in the next year.
A survey by an unrelated polling organization shows that the public is generally receptive to the idea of trying new types of tea.
The Survey Group is funded by a consortium of consumer advocacy groups.
The stores from which the Survey Group collected information about tea sales are all located in the same small region of the country.
Tea has been the subject of an expensive and efficient advertising campaign funded, in part, by the National Tea Association.

notes.body: A survey the Association only plans to run next year gives us no data now. Announcing a survey isn't evidence of anything, and it doesn't touch the Survey Group's 20 years of flat sales. Even if the new survey comes out differently, A doesn't tell us that.

Being "generally receptive to the idea of trying new types of tea" is an attitude, not a purchase, and it isn't a change over time. The public could have been just as receptive 20 years ago. Barr's conclusion is about tea being more popular now than before, and B gives no before-and-after comparison.

C is trying to make us doubt the Survey Group. But why would consumer advocacy groups want tea sales to look flat? C gives no motive, and the stimulus calls the Survey Group neutral. Funding alone, with no reason to skew the data, doesn't weaken the survey.

This is the excuse for the survey data we predicted. If every surveyed store is "located in the same small region of the country," flat sales there tell us very little about the country as a whole. Tea could be booming everywhere else.

The move to repeat: when the evidence is a survey or a sample, weaken by showing the sample doesn't represent the group the conclusion is about.

E is the tempting one because an "expensive and efficient advertising campaign" sounds like it should boost popularity. But it tells us about effort, not results, and Barr's data says sales didn't move. If anything, E helps Barr: it explains the visibility the Association cited as paid advertising, so that visibility is weaker evidence that people actually like tea more.

The National Tea Association has announced that it plans to carry out its own retail survey in the next year.
A survey by an unrelated polling organization shows that the public is generally receptive to the idea of trying new types of tea.
The Survey Group is funded by a consortium of consumer advocacy groups.
The stores from which the Survey Group collected information about tea sales are all located in the same small region of the country.
Tea has been the subject of an expensive and efficient advertising campaign funded, in part, by the National Tea Association.

notes.body: The Tea Association announcing it will do a survey next year is just news about a future event. It tells us nothing about whether tea is more popular now or whether the Survey Group's data is reliable. To weaken Barr we need something that calls his evidence into question, not something that mentions the other side.

This sounds like it might help, but watch the gap. The public being "receptive to the idea of trying" new teas is a measure of attitude, not behavior. Barr's argument is built on actual sales numbers. People can say they are open to something and still never buy it. So this answer does not actually contradict Barr's evidence.

This might feel like a "the data is biased" answer, but it is not. The stimulus already says the Survey Group is neutral, and the answer does not actually allege bias — it just names the funder. Without a story about how consumer advocacy funding would distort tea sales numbers, this leaves Barr's evidence intact.

Here is the weakener. Barr's entire case rides on the Survey Group's sales data. If those stores are all in one tiny corner of the country, then "no change in tea sales" only tells us about that corner — not about the country as a whole.

It is like trying to figure out whether a band is getting more popular nationwide by checking ticket sales at one venue in one city. Even if those numbers are flat, the band could be exploding everywhere else.

The Tea Association's claim that tea is getting more popular nationally could easily still be right; Barr just has not actually disproved it.

A big ad campaign is the kind of thing the Tea Association would point to in its argument that tea is getting more popular — but advertising is effort, not result. Barr's whole point is that the sales numbers stayed flat *despite* all that visibility. Telling us the ad campaign was big and efficient does not show sales actually moved.

choices.text: Fatima was a mathematician who often thought about unsolved problems of mathematics, although it was unpleasant to be reminded that most would probably remain unsolved in her lifetime. As the saying goes, “Strange how much you’ve got to know before you know how little you know.”

Harold’s friends were surprised when he revealed that he had left his wallet at home and asked that someone lend him money. But he had done the same thing many times before. As Halliard said, “The force of selfishness is as inevitable and as calculable as the force of gravitation. ”

The best model of vacuum cleaner was the most expensive on the market, but it would have made Roger unhappy to purchase it. For although he never wanted anything but the best, he was also quite frugal, and would never have forgiven himself for spending the money. As the saying goes, “A penny saved is a penny earned.”
Sharon loved cats, but her husband was allergic to them. Still, he was occasionally willing to accompany her to cat shows. As the saying goes, “Shared lives mean shared loves. ”

Raoul spent a year planning and preparing for a fantastic ski trip. He enjoyed his ski trip greatly until he broke his leg and had to spend two weeks in the hospital. As the saying goes, “All’s well that ends well.”

notes.body: Fatima knows enough mathematics to see how much will stay unsolved. That's the saying in action: you need to know a lot before you see how little you know. The story illustrates it, so the phrase is used properly.

Harold has done the same thing many times before. That's selfishness as predictable as gravity, so the quote matches the story. The friends' surprise doesn't change that Harold's behavior was calculable.

Roger won't buy the expensive vacuum because Roger is frugal and would never forgive the spending. "A penny saved is a penny earned" is the frugal person's motto, so the story illustrates it and the phrase is used properly.

Sharon loves cats, and Sharon's husband, despite the allergy, still sometimes comes along to cat shows. Sharing a life with Sharon means sharing what Sharon loves, at least a little. The story illustrates the saying.

Raoul's trip ended with a broken leg and two weeks in the hospital. That didn't end well, so "All's well that ends well" has no illustration here. The story is an apparent counterexample, and putting "as the saying goes" after it is the misuse the principle describes.

notes.body: Fatima is a mathematician confronted by the vastness of what nobody has solved. The saying is about realizing how much you have to know before you can grasp how little you know. That is actually a reasonable match — the story illustrates the proverb. So this usage is fine, not inappropriate.

Harold's wallet-forgetting trick is something he has done many times. The saying treats selfishness as predictable — like gravity. The story matches the saying: a reliable, predictable instance of selfishness. Used appropriately.
Roger's situation — choosing not to buy because he values frugality — is a textbook illustration of "a penny saved is a penny earned." The story and the saying line up. Used appropriately.

Sharon's husband going to cat shows despite his allergy is exactly the kind of "you take on what your partner loves" behavior the saying describes. The story illustrates the saying. Used appropriately.

Look at how Raoul's story actually ends: a broken leg and two weeks in the hospital. That is the opposite of "all's well that ends well." The trip did not end well at all.

The principle says "as the saying goes" should follow a story that illustrates the saying. Here the story is the reverse — a counterexample. Using "as the saying goes" to introduce a saying that the story contradicts is exactly the inappropriate usage the principle warns about.

choices.text: National resources should be regulated by international agreement when wildlife is endangered.
The right of future generations to have wildlife preserved supersedes the economic needs of individual nations.
Only when a reduction of populations of endangered species by commercial development has been found should regulation be implemented to prevent further damage.
Environment regulation must aim at preventing any further environmental damage and cannot allow for the different degrees to which different nations have already harmed the environment.
It is imprudent to allow further depletion of natural resources.

notes.body: The Development Commission claims Figoria has "as much right to govern our own resources" as other countries. Handing regulation to an international agreement takes that right away, and the trigger, endangered wildlife, is the Wildlife Commission's whole case. A works against the side it is supposed to help.

The Development Commission's case rests partly on growth, which is an economic need. B says the right of future generations to preserved wildlife outranks "the economic needs of individual nations," so that appeal loses. This is a principle the Wildlife Commission would cite, not the Development Commission.

C says regulation should happen only when a reduction of endangered species by commercial development "has been found." Flip that around: if no such reduction has been found, no regulation yet. The Development Commission says Figoria has conserved and that its development "might not affect wildlife," so no harm has been found in Figoria. The Wildlife Commission wants regulation before any harm, based on damage in other nations. C rules that out.

That is the move when a principle question asks you to support one side against the other: find the exact point where the two sides split, then pick the principle whose condition the favored side's evidence satisfies.

This is the trap. It talks about how different nations have harmed the environment to different degrees. That's the Development Commission's theme, so it feels like their answer. But read what it concludes: regulation cannot allow for those differences. The commission's whole complaint is that Figoria's record of conserving should count. D says it doesn't.

Developing wetlands depletes a natural resource. If further depletion is "imprudent," the development the Development Commission is asking for is imprudent too. E gives the Wildlife Commission a reason to restrict development, which is the opposite of what we need.

National resources should be regulated by international agreement when wildlife is endangered.
The right of future generations to have wildlife preserved supersedes the economic needs of individual nations.
Only when a reduction of populations of endangered species by commercial development has been found should regulation be implemented to prevent further damage.
Environment regulation must aim at preventing any further environmental damage and cannot allow for the different degrees to which different nations have already harmed the environment.
It is imprudent to allow further depletion of natural resources.

notes.body: This principle is about who should regulate (international agreements). The actual debate is whether Figoria should regulate at all, given that wildlife "might not" be affected. The principle does not pick a winner between the two sides.

This principle says preserving wildlife matters more than meeting current economic needs. That is exactly the opposite of what the Development Commission is arguing — they are saying growth is necessary and the wildlife impact is uncertain. This principle would crush their position, not strengthen it.

This is the principle the Development Commission needs. It says regulation only kicks in once a population has actually been reduced by commercial development.

Apply that to Figoria: no reduction has happened yet (Figoria has conserved), and the planned development "might not" affect wildlife. Under this rule, regulation is not yet justified — so the Development Commission's "let us develop" position wins.

The Wildlife Commission's precautionary, regulate-up-front stance directly conflicts with this principle, which is the contrast the question is looking for.

Read this carefully — it actually undercuts the Development Commission. They wanted special treatment *because* Figoria has not yet harmed wetlands like other nations have. This principle says you cannot give that kind of credit; everyone must just prevent further damage. That favors immediate regulation, which is the Wildlife Commission's position.

This principle treats further depletion as imprudent — full stop. The Development Commission wants to be allowed to deplete (develop) some wetlands. So this principle opposes their position rather than supporting it.

choices.text: Regular afternoon exercise is one of the things required for adequate deep-sleep.
Exercise in the morning is almost as likely to have as many beneficial effects on sleep as is exercise in the afternoon.
The best way to get increased deep-sleep is to induce a slight increase in body temperature just before bedtime.
No one in the control group experienced a rise in body temperature just before bedtime.
Raising body temperature slightly by taking a warm bath just before bedtime will likely result in increased deep-sleep.

notes.body: "Required" means no one gets adequate deep sleep without afternoon exercise. The study only shows that exercisers got more deep sleep than a group that exercised little or not at all. And the mechanism points the other way: if heat is the cause, other sources of heat could do the job without exercise.

The mechanism depends on body heat lasting until after bedtime. Morning exercise never comes up, and its heat could easily wear off long before night. Nothing lets us compare morning exercise with afternoon exercise.
"The best way" needs a comparison with every other way to get deep sleep. The researcher describes one thing that helps. That supports "this works," not "nothing works better."

This is the most popular wrong answer. "No one" covers every person in the control group. They exercised little, but someone could have been warmed by a hot meal or a fever. The study reports group results, not every individual.

The researcher says deeper sleep comes from "this extra heat," a slight rise in body temperature that lasts past bedtime. A warm bath just before bed produces that same condition, so the mechanism predicts it should help too. Notice the move: when a stimulus names the mechanism behind a result, the supported answer often applies that mechanism to a new case. "Will likely" is as strong as the mechanism allows, and no stronger.

notes.body: Watch the word "required." That word means you cannot get adequate deep sleep without afternoon exercise. The study only showed that afternoon exercisers got *more* deep sleep than non-exercisers — it never said the non-exercisers were sleep-deprived. Plenty of people without afternoon exercise routines presumably sleep just fine.

The mechanism specifically depends on the temperature boost lasting until bedtime. Morning exercise might wear off long before then. Since the stimulus says nothing about morning exercise, we cannot conclude it is almost as effective as afternoon exercise.

Notice "the best way." For something to be the best, you would have to know about all the alternatives and rule them out. The stimulus only describes one mechanism that works. There could be other methods — sleep medications, cool rooms, blackout curtains — that work even better. We have no evidence to rank them.

"No one" is a sweeping claim about every single person in the control group. The stimulus only tells us about averages. Some control-group members could easily have had a body-temperature bump from a warm meal, a hot bath, or even being a little sick. The data does not exclude that.

This is the answer that respects the mechanism. The researcher said the deep sleep comes from the slight body-temperature rise that lasts until past bedtime. So what really matters is the temperature, not the exercise.

A warm bath right before bed produces exactly that condition: a small temperature boost going into bedtime. So we would expect a similar effect on deep sleep.

Notice the hedged language too — "will likely result." That matches what the stimulus actually supports. No overreach.

choices.text: It makes a generalization about Egyptian society based on a sample so small that it is likely to be unrepresentative.
It uses the term “alcoholic beverage” in a different sense in the premises than in the conclusion.
It presumes, without providing justification, that because one society developed a technology before another, the development in the latter was dependent on the development in the former.
It ignores the possibility that the first known instance of a kind is not the first instance of that kind.
It provides no evidence for the claim that the Babylonians produced wine as early as 1500 B.C.

notes.body: A generalization flaw would need a claim about Egyptian society as a whole, such as how common beer drinking was. The conclusion isn't about that. One cup is enough to show alcohol was being made in Egypt by 2000 B.C. The real question is whether anyone made it before then.

The term holds steady. The premises mention Babylonian wine and Egyptian beer, and the conclusion's "alcoholic beverages" covers both in the same sense. Nothing shifts meaning between premises and conclusion. The argument compares dates, so the weak spot is about what came first, not what the words mean.

The argument never says Babylonian wine-making depended on Egyptian brewing. It claims only that Egypt came first in time. C describes a claim about one society's technology depending on another's, and the author makes no such claim, so there is nothing for this criticism to attack.

This is the gap we predicted. "The first known instance of a kind" is the 2000 B.C. Egyptian cup, the oldest evidence found so far. "The first instance of that kind" is what the conclusion claims: the Egyptians were the first society ever to produce alcohol. The author treats the two as the same. Test it: could some society have made alcohol before 2000 B.C. without leaving evidence we have found? Yes, and the Babylonians losing their title shows new finds can overturn an old first. When a Flaw conclusion claims a first, look for this answer.

Arguments may state background facts without proving them, and the 1500 B.C. date mainly tells us what used to be believed. Supporting it wouldn't help the argument anyway: even a well-documented Babylonian date can't show that no society produced alcohol before 2000 B.C. The flaw is elsewhere.

notes.body: Sampling flaws happen when you draw a broad conclusion about a population from too few examples. Here the argument is not generalizing about Egyptian society — it is making a single comparative claim about who came first. The cup is one piece of evidence, not a sample. This is naming a flaw the argument does not commit.

Equivocation means using the same word in two different senses. Here "alcoholic beverage" covers both Babylonian wine and Egyptian beer in the same sense. There is no slippery word swap between evidence and conclusion. Wrong flaw.

This describes an "earlier developer caused the later developer" flaw. The argument never says the Babylonians got fermentation from the Egyptians — only that the Egyptians did it first. There is no claim of causation or dependence to attack. Wrong flaw.

This is the right diagnosis. The author found the oldest piece of evidence we have for alcohol production. That is not the same as showing Egyptians were the first ever.

Think of it this way: the oldest written document we have ever discovered is not necessarily the very first document anyone ever wrote. Maybe earlier ones existed and got destroyed, or maybe we just have not found them yet. The same problem applies here.

The argument leaps from "oldest evidence we have" to "first ever." That is the flaw, and this answer names it precisely.

The Babylonian-wine claim is the conventional view the argument is replacing. Even if we just accept it on faith, the argument still works as written: 2000 B.C. is older than 1500 B.C. So failing to provide evidence for the Babylonian date is not the actual flaw — and it is also not really a flaw, since the argument is treating that as background.

choices.text: The behavior of organisms with elaborate brain mechanisms is usually not instinctual.
Insect behavior is exclusively instinctual.
All organisms with brains larger than insects’ brains are capable of some measure of flexible behavior.
All organisms with large brains are biologically equipped for flexible behavior.
Only organisms with brains of insect size or smaller engage in purely instinctual behavior.

notes.body: "Usually not instinctual" is a claim about how organisms with elaborate brains actually behave. The stimulus gives a requirement for flexible behavior, so it can only tell us who can't behave flexibly. An organism with plenty of neurons could still run on instinct most of the time without breaking any statement.

Run the chain from insects. No insect brain provides a sufficiently large number of neurons, and flexible behavior requires one, so no insect brain is capable of flexible behavior. The stimulus defines flexible as noninstinctual, so whatever insects do is instinctual.

"Exclusively" sounds strong, but it's earned: the requirement is missing for every insect, so there is no room for even a little flexible behavior. When a strong word shows up on Must Be True, check whether a universal rule (here, "no insect brain") backs it before crossing it off.

Larger than an insect's brain isn't the same as large enough. The stimulus only says insect brains fall short. A brain could beat an insect's and still lack the neurons. And even a brain with enough neurons isn't guaranteed flexible behavior, because the neuron count is a requirement, not a guarantee.

This reverses the rule. Capable of flexible behavior → large number of neurons says the neurons are required. D reads it as large brain → equipped for flexible behavior, treating the requirement as enough. Driving legally requires a license, but holding a license doesn't make someone a driver. D also swaps "large brain" for "large number of neurons," which the stimulus never equates.

E says purely instinctual → brain of insect size or smaller. We only know the other direction: insect → instinctual. An organism with a bigger brain that still falls short of the neuron count would also be limited to instinct, and nothing rules that out. "Only" makes a small brain a requirement for pure instinct, and the stimulus never sets that requirement.

The behavior of organisms with elaborate brain mechanisms is usually not instinctual.
Insect behavior is exclusively instinctual.
All organisms with brains larger than insects’ brains are capable of some measure of flexible behavior.
All organisms with large brains are biologically equipped for flexible behavior.
Only organisms with brains of insect size or smaller engage in purely instinctual behavior.

notes.body: This claims that elaborate-brain organisms *usually* behave non-instinctually. The passage tells us they have the capacity for flexible behavior, but it never says how often they use it. They could spend most of their time on instinct and only occasionally use flexibility. The "usually" is unsupported.

This is exactly the inference the chain forces. The passage gives a clean two-option dichotomy: behavior is instinctual or flexible (noninstinctual). Flexible behavior needs many neurons. Insect brains don't have many.

So insects can't do flexible behavior. The only kind they can do is instinctual. That makes their behavior exclusively instinctual — which is exactly what (B) says.

The passage tells us insect brains fall below the neuron threshold for flexible behavior. It says nothing about whether *every* non-insect organism clears that threshold. Plenty of small animals might still have brains too small for flexibility. "All organisms with brains larger than insects'" is much too sweeping.

The passage requires "a large number of neurons" for flexible behavior. This answer talks about "large brains," which isn't quite the same — different organisms pack neurons differently, and not every large-brained organism has the right kind of neuron density. The passage also doesn't commit to "all" large-brained organisms being capable.

This answer says only insect-or-smaller-brained organisms do purely instinctual behavior. The passage tells us insects fall below the neuron threshold, so they're instinct-only. But it doesn't say no other animal does. There could be non-insect animals also limited to instinct. The "only" is too strong.

choices.text: The manipulation of the genetic code of organisms is never unethical.
Anything that is accomplished by nature is not unethical to accomplish with science.
The manipulation of the genetic code through selective breeding for desired traits is not unethical.
The manipulation of the genetic code through selective breeding for desired traits is important for human survival.
Science can accomplish only what is already in some sense natural, and nothing natural is unethical.

notes.body: "Never" is far more than the argument needs. The scientist's evidence is about one kind of manipulation, selective breeding. Negate A: some manipulation of genetic codes is unethical, say, manipulation done to cause harm. The scientist can accept that and still argue that genetic engineering, like selective breeding, is not unethical.

B is tempting because it sounds like a defense of genetic engineering. But the scientist's evidence is selective breeding, something people did, not something nature accomplished. Negate B: some things nature accomplishes would be unethical to accomplish with science. The comparison between breeding and genetic engineering is untouched.

Negate it: "selective breeding for desired traits is unethical." Then the analogy turns against the scientist. Showing that genetic engineering is like selective breeding only puts it next to something unethical, and the millennia of practice just mean we've been doing something wrong for a long time. The conclusion falls.

The move: in an argument by analogy, the conclusion borrows a property from the comparison case. The argument has to assume the comparison case actually has that property.

The argument is about ethics, not usefulness. Negate D: selective breeding is not important for human survival. Breeding could still be ethical, and the analogy still works. Something can be unimportant and perfectly acceptable.

E makes two sweeping claims: science can do only what is natural, and nothing natural is unethical. The scientist relies on neither. Negate E, say, science can do some things that aren't natural, and the comparison between selective breeding and genetic engineering still stands.

notes.body: "Never unethical" is a sweeping claim about every imaginable case. The argument does not need that. It just needs the specific kind of manipulation involved in genetic engineering (and the selective-breeding precedent) to be okay. If you negate this and admit that some genetic manipulation is unethical, the scientist can still argue that *this* kind is fine.

This answer puts the argument on a different foundation — "if nature does it, science can do it." But the scientist is not arguing from nature; the scientist is arguing from a long-standing human practice (selective breeding). The argument can succeed without this principle, so it is not assumed.

This is the assumption the argument cannot do without. The scientist's entire defense is: "Selective breeding is genetic engineering, we have been doing it for millennia, so genetic engineering is not unethical."

That move only works if selective breeding itself is not unethical. If you negate this answer — say, "selective breeding actually is unethical" — then "we have been doing it for millennia" no longer saves anything. It just means humans have been doing something unethical for a long time. The conclusion collapses.

That negation test ("argument falls apart when negated") is exactly the test for a necessary assumption.

The argument is purely about ethics, not importance. Even if selective breeding turned out to be totally unimportant for human survival, the scientist's argument still works the same way: it is a long-standing practice that, if ethical, transfers ethical cover to genetic engineering. Importance does not enter the picture.

This answer makes a sweeping claim about nature and what science can do. The scientist's argument is much narrower — it just needs selective breeding to be acceptable. The argument can succeed without this universal principle, so it is not necessary.

choices.text: How much more salt than is contained in a rat’s normal diet was there in the high-salt diet?
Did the high blood pressure have any adverse health effects on those rats that developed it?
What percentage of naturally occurring rat colonies feed on high-salt diets?
How many rats in the colony studied had abnormally high blood pressure before the study began?
Have other species of rodents been used in experiments of the same kind?

notes.body: Imagine two answers: twice the normal salt, or ten times. Either way, we still don't know whether the rats had high blood pressure before the study. The amount of salt tells us how big the dose was, not whether the dose did anything.

Suppose the high blood pressure caused serious harm, or none at all. The conclusion is only that high-salt diets are linked to high blood pressure. What high blood pressure does afterward can't tell us whether salt produced it.

How many wild colonies eat salty food tells us how common the diet is, not what it does. Whether the answer is 1 percent or 90 percent, this study's evidence for a link is exactly as strong as before.

This is the before-measurement the study is missing. Run both answers. If most of the colony already had abnormally high blood pressure, the after-numbers show nothing about salt and the conclusion falls apart. If almost none did, a jump to 75 percent points straight at the diet.

One question, two answers, opposite effects on the conclusion: that's what a relevant Evaluate question does. Next time a study reports only results after a treatment, ask what the numbers were before it.
Yes or no, other rodent experiments say nothing about this colony. Even a yes wouldn't tell us what those experiments found, and the conclusion is about rats anyway.

notes.body: This question asks how much salt was in the diet. But the argument's real problem is whether the rats started out with high blood pressure to begin with. Knowing the exact dosage does not help us answer that — whether it was 5 times or 10 times normal salt, we still need the baseline.

The conclusion is just about whether salt is connected to high blood pressure. Whether high blood pressure then leads to other health problems is a separate question. It does not help us evaluate the salt-to-blood-pressure link.

This asks about wild rat populations. The study is a lab experiment. Even if we knew that 0% or 100% of wild rats eat high-salt diets, that would not tell us anything about whether these specific lab rats had high blood pressure when the study started.

This is the question that has to be asked. The whole argument turns on whether the diet actually changed the rats' blood pressure or whether the rats already had high blood pressure to begin with.

Imagine the answer: "Most of the rats had high blood pressure before the study." Now the salt diet has not been shown to cause anything; the high blood pressure was already there.

Now imagine the opposite: "Almost none of the rats had high blood pressure before the study." Now the diet looks like it really did something — three-quarters of them developed high blood pressure during the study. The whole conclusion swings on this answer.

The conclusion is about rats — not rodents in general. Whether mice or hamsters have been studied does not touch the central question of whether *these* rats already had high blood pressure when the experiment began.

choices.text: demonstrating that Barr Motor Company has more repeat customers than its competitors
using an analogy to reach the conclusion that Barr Motor Company is superior to its competitors
proving that Barr Motor Company has a long- standing tradition of pride
understating the role that pride plays in accounting for the success of Austin Stables
asserting that Barr Motor Company has an older tradition of pride than does Austin Stables

notes.body: The ad never mentions customers, repeat or otherwise. Its only evidence is pride and winning. A Method answer has to describe what the argument actually does, and nothing in the ad demonstrates anything about who comes back to buy.

Check both halves. Conclusion: "superior to its competitors" matches "produce more winning automobiles than our competitors." Evidence: "using an analogy" matches the Austin Stables comparison. Pride made Austin beat other stables; Barr has similar pride; so Barr will beat other car makers.

When an argument borrows a result from one situation and claims it for a similar one, expect the Method answer to say analogy.

C names something the ad does say: Barr has shown pride "For generations." But the ad only asserts it; nothing in the ad proves it. And it is a premise, not where the ad is going. The ad's point is that Barr will out-win its competitors. Asserting a premise and proving a claim are different moves, and a Method answer has to describe the argument's actual work.

The ad credits pride fully: pride "accounts for" Austin's success. It plays pride's role up, not down. Understating it would undercut the ad's own analogy, since Barr's case rests on pride being what makes the difference.

The ad never compares the ages of the two traditions. It says Barr has shown pride "For generations" and calls Austin's pride a tradition, but it never says which is older. The analogy needs the pride to be similar, not older.

choices.text: takes for granted that there is a causal connection between the hippocampus and being in a state of profound creativity
fails to consider that music is not necessary for one to be in a state of profound creativity
does not rule out the possibility that listening to music by means other than a tape recording also increases theta waves
ignores the possibility that an increase in theta waves may not always be accompanied by a state of profound creativity
provides insufficient reasons to believe that people who are not in states of profound creativity have low levels of theta brain waves

notes.body: The hippocampus is just one of the regions where theta waves occur. The argument never needs the hippocampus to cause anything; its leap is from theta waves to creativity. Delete the hippocampus from the stimulus and the flaw is still there.
The columnist says music is *enough* for creativity, not that it is *required*. Pointing out that people can be creative without music agrees with everything the columnist said.
If live music or a phone speaker also raises theta waves, that is perfectly consistent with the argument. It would only widen the conclusion, not undermine it.

The rule is creativity → more theta waves. The columnist runs it backward: more theta waves → creativity. Ask, "Could theta waves rise without creativity showing up?" If yes, music can raise theta waves and leave you no more creative than before. A fever comes with a rising temperature, but warming up in a sauna does not give you a fever.

This one is close, so check the wording. The evidence and conclusion are about an *increase* in theta waves. (E) is about people having *low levels* of them. Someone could start with moderate theta levels, get an increase from music, and still not be creative. The gap is whether an increase guarantees creativity, which (D) states directly; a claim about baseline levels does not capture it.

notes.body: The hippocampus is just one location mentioned where theta waves occur — the argument is not pinning anything on it. The flaw is elsewhere: in the leap from "creativity comes with theta waves" to "theta waves produce creativity." This answer attacks the wrong target.

This says the argument missed that music is not needed for creativity. But the argument's conclusion is that one *can* attain creativity by listening to music — not that music is the only path. Even if there are other paths, the conclusion can still be valid. So pointing this out is not a real objection to the argument.

This raises a question about music delivery methods. It does not actually undermine the argument — even if live music also raises theta waves, that does not make tape-recorded music ineffective. The argument's conclusion only requires tapes to work, and this objection does not show they do not.

Here is the real flaw. The stimulus tells us creativity is accompanied by theta waves. That means: when creativity is happening, theta waves are up. It does *not* tell us the reverse — that whenever theta waves are up, creativity is happening.

So music can spike theta waves without spiking creativity. Maybe relaxation, daydreaming, or zoning out also raises theta waves. The argument needed the reverse direction (theta waves → creativity) and never proved it.

This answer pinpoints exactly that: the increase in theta waves may not always come with creativity.
This faults the argument for not establishing what theta waves look like in non-creative people. But the argument never makes that claim. It is not a flaw to fail to support a claim you never made.

choices.text: Among the first-graders who received the after-school lessons in handwriting, those who practiced the most learned to write letters the most automatically.

The first-graders who wrote letters the most automatically before receiving the after-school lessons in handwriting showed the greatest improvement in their composition skills over the course of the lessons.
Over the course of the lessons, the first-graders who showed greater improvement in their ability to write letters automatically also generally showed greater improvement in their composition skills.

Before receiving the after-school lessons in handwriting, the 100 first-graders who received the lessons were representative of first-graders more generally, with respect to their skills in both handwriting and composition.
Among the first-graders who received the lessons in handwriting, those who started out with strong composition skills showed substantial improvement in how automatically they could write letters.

notes.body: This connects practice to automatic handwriting. That just tells us how kids became automatic. Composition never appears, so it does nothing to show that automatic writing frees up mental resources for other activities.

This one tempts because it links automatic writing with composition gains. But it is about kids who were already automatic before the lessons, and that fits both stories equally well: automatic writers had attention free, or they were simply stronger students who would improve at composition anyway. An answer that fits the rival as well as the author's story can't favor the author. B never shows that becoming more automatic did anything.

This is the prediction. The evidence only said the best improvers ended up most automatic. C says the kids whose automaticity improved more also generally improved more at composition. Now the gain in one skill tracks the gain in the other during the same lessons, which is what the author's story predicts and what the stronger-students story doesn't need.

The move: when a study's evidence compares a starting trait with an improvement, look for an answer that turns it into change matching change.

A representative group helps us apply the results to first-graders in general. It doesn't touch the real question, which is whether automatic handwriting causes the composition gains or something else explains both.

This runs the other way. Kids who started with strong composition skills became much more automatic, which hints that composition skill (or general ability) drives automaticity. That's a rival story, not support for the author's one.

notes.body: This just says the kids who practiced more got more automatic at writing. The argument is not about practice — it is about whether automatic handwriting frees up the brain for composition. This answer does not bring composition into the picture at all.

This answer is about kids who started the lessons with automatic handwriting already. The argument is about kids whose handwriting *became* automatic during the lessons. Pre-existing automaticity is a different claim from gains in automaticity.

This is the strengthener. The argument's story is that getting more automatic at handwriting frees up the brain for other tasks like composition. If that story is right, we would expect bigger handwriting gains to come with bigger composition gains — and that is exactly what this answer tells us.

Original evidence: the top composition-improvers were also the most automatic. This answer adds: across all the lesson-takers, the relationship goes both ways — more automatic gains, more composition gains.

That covariation is direct support for the proposed mechanism.

This says the kids in the study were a normal sample of first-graders. That helps us trust the result generalizes — but it does not strengthen the underlying causal claim about why handwriting automaticity helps composition. We still need evidence about how the two skills relate to each other.

Read this carefully — it actually points away from the conclusion. The argument is "automatic handwriting causes composition gains." This answer says the kids with strong composition to start were the ones who got more automatic. That suggests composition might be driving handwriting gains, not the other way around. That is the opposite of what we want.

choices.text: Anybody who has a dog knows the true value of companionship, and Alicia has demonstrated that she knows the true value of companionship; thus we can safely conclude that Alicia has a dog.

Anyone who discovers something new is someone who has examined all the possible solutions to a problem. Fran has surely never discovered something new. Therefore, Fran has never explored all the possible solutions to a problem.

Any person who does not face sufficient challenges is a person who does not accomplish everything he or she can. Jill is a person who accomplishes everything she can, so Jill is a person who faces sufficient challenges.

By definition, a polygon is any closed plane figure bounded by straight lines. That object pictured on the chalkboard is certainly a closed plane figure bounded by a large number of straight lines, so that object pictured on the chalkboard must be a polygon.

People who have never lost something that they cannot afford to lose will be lax about keeping their property secure. Jon is lax about keeping property secure when it is something he can afford to lose, so Jon must never have lost anything.

notes.body:
A matches piece for piece. Rule: has a dog → knows the true value of companionship. Fact: Alicia has demonstrated knowing the true value of companionship, the right side. Conclusion: Alicia has a dog, the left side. That is the original's reversal exactly: observe the result, conclude the trigger. Alicia might value companionship because of friends, family or a cat.

The move to repeat: on a conditional parallel flaw question, diagram the rule, then check that the evidence and the conclusion land on the same sides of the arrow as in the original.

B diagrams as discovers something new → examined all possible solutions. Fran never discovered something new, which negates the left side, and the conclusion negates the right side. That is denying the trigger: a flaw, but not the original's, which affirmed the result. B also slides from examined to explored.

C is the topic lure: challenges and accomplishing everything sound like the original. Diagram it. Not sufficient challenges → does not accomplish everything one can. Jill accomplishes everything, which negates the right side, so Jill faces sufficient challenges, the negated left side. That is a valid contrapositive, and a parallel flaw answer has to be flawed.

D starts from a definition, and a definition runs both ways: every polygon is a closed plane figure bounded by straight lines, and every such figure is a polygon. So moving from the description to the label is valid. A large number of straight lines is still straight lines. There is no flaw here to match.

E is the closest trap, because it also seems to move from a result to a trigger. But the pieces do not line up. The rule's result is being lax about keeping property secure; the evidence shows Jon lax about property Jon can afford to lose, a narrower claim. The rule's trigger is never having lost something one cannot afford to lose; the conclusion is that Jon never lost anything at all. Both pieces drift from the rule's terms, so E is not the clean reversal the original makes. A copies it exactly.

notes.body:
This is the parallel flaw. Map it onto the original:

**Original:** Never-pushed → underperforming. Alex is underperforming. So Alex was never pushed.

**This answer:** Has a dog → knows companionship. Alicia knows companionship. So Alicia has a dog.

Same form, same mistake. Knowing companionship has many possible sources (friends, family, cats), just as underperformance has many sources. Picking just one cause because the result happened is the flaw — affirming the consequent — and this answer commits it identically.

Map this one out: discoverer → examined all solutions. Fran is not a discoverer (denying antecedent). Conclusion: Fran has not explored all solutions (denying consequent). This is a different mistake from the original. The original moves from observed effect to assumed cause; this one moves from "no cause" to "no effect." Wrong shape.

This argument is actually valid. "Not challenged → not accomplishing all" — and Jill accomplishes all. By contrapositive, she must be challenged. That is solid reasoning. We need a flawed parallel, not a valid one.

This argument applies a definition correctly. "A polygon is X. This object is X. So this object is a polygon." That is not flawed — definitions work biconditionally (anything fitting the definition is a polygon, anything that is a polygon fits the definition). Valid reasoning, so not a parallel to the flawed original.

This one gets messy — the conditional is about losing something irreplaceable, but Jon is described as lax with replaceable things, and the conclusion is he never lost *anything*. The scope keeps shifting in ways the original does not. The structure does not cleanly mirror the original's "premise → consequent observed → antecedent concluded" pattern.
